catalog_quote: Stress in LG is assigned within the ‘three syllable window’. This means that the stressed syllable must be one of the three last syllables in a PrWd. Within this window, stress occurs according to the language-specific stress pattern. The findings for LG are such that superheavy syllables (i.e. syllables with more than two positions) receive stress even in final position. If the final syllable is not heavy at the surface level, trochaic stress is assigned generally to the rightmost non-final heavy syllable or else to the rightmost non-final sequence of two light syllables. Syllables containing a schwa in the nucleus remain unstressed at all times. Stress in loanwords differs from this pattern by means of lexically pre-determined stress markings. (p. 122) ... If the final syllable is not heavy at the surface level, trochaic stress is assigned generally to the rightmost non-final heavy syllable or els…
new_statements.rule_in_words: Primary stress falls within the last three syllables: on the penult if it is closed (CVC, heavy); if the penult is open (CV, counted light) stress moves to the antepenult; a superheavy final syllable (CVVC/CVCC with extrasyllabic final C) takes final stress; schwa syllables are never stressed. Prehn's own summary (p. 154): 'The stress assignment is such that if the penultimate syllable is (C)VC, stress goes there; if the respective penultimate syllable is (C)V the stress moves further to the left to the antepenult. [..] Word-final stress occurs either in mono- and bisyllables that comprise a light initial syllable and a heavy final syllable, or in cases with final superheavy syllable. The preferred foot structure is a moraic trochee. All in all, the major part of the LG stress assignment is predictable by means of syllable weight in this way.' The reference grammar Lindow et al. (1998:30), as reported by Prehn p. 123, states instead that stress is generally on the initial syllable; Prehn argues that the initial-stress examples are actually penultimate-CVC cases and old compounds. In native vocabulary the two accounts mostly coincide (root/initial = penult or antepenult).
new_statements.secondary_stress: Explicitly excluded from the analysis: 'Compound and phrasal stress is not considered in the analysis, and secondary stress only where necessary' (p. 121).
new_statements.exceptions: Romance/other loanwords with lexically fixed stress (e.g. [k'jyt] 'cabin', [k'p l] 'chapel', sombrero, bikini) — final or penultimate stress insensitive to weight (pp. 145-154); bisyllables with light initial + heavy final syllable take final stress (Table 24b); old compounds like 'hedgehog' (Swin+Egel) show initial stress (fn. 120). Author's caveat p. 145: 'the analyzed data is rather limited and, thus, is not entirely conclusive.'
new_statements.domain_note: Prosodic word (PrWd), citation forms of simplex words; data drawn largely from Lindow 1984 (dictionary) and Niekerken 1935 plus the author's recordings from Kirchwerder, Altenwerder (Hamburg) and Alfstedt (near Bremervörde, Lower Saxony). Phrasal and compound stress not treated.
new_statements.identity_note: The first-hand statement (Prehn 2012) describes North Low Saxon of the Hamburg Elbe-Marsch villages Kirchwerder and Altenwerder and of Alfstedt near Bremervörde (Lower Saxony) — i.e. Nordniedersächsisch proper, which nort2628 'German Northern Low Saxon' covers — not the East Frisian Low Saxon dialect that ISO 639-3 frs specifically denotes (Glottolog folds East Frisian Low German into nort2628; no separate glottocode found). The initial-stress claim (Lindow et al. 1998:30) is for Low German generally. No opened source states stress for the East Frisian subdialect itself; Hobbing 1879 (Greetsiel, East Frisia) is silent on stress position.

sources.note: Chapter 4 'Low German stress' (pp. 121-154): primary word stress is weight-sensitive within a three-syllable window; stress on the penult if it is CVC, otherwise on the antepenult; final stress only on superheavy finals (and a small set of light+heavy bisyllables / Romance loans with lexical stress); schwa syllables never stressed; reports Lindow et al. 1998:30 as stating initial stress (p. 123) and argues the real pattern is weight-based.
